3.text: are old and worn (Fig. 55). Besides bone

4.text: and ivory balls, wooden ones were also used.

5.text: These had the advantage of not sinking

6.text: when they fell into the water.

7.text: The bird-dart is used along the Arctic

8.text: shore for the killing of moulting ducks and

9.text: geese, on the Kolyma, alike by the Chuk-

10.text: chee and by the Russianized Yukaghir

11.text: (Fig. 56); on Bering Sea, only by the Rus-

12.text: sianized natives of the Middle Anadyr, who

13.text: brought it over from the Kolyma. How-

14.text: ever, on old house-sites in Wuteˊen and
14.note: that's the descender of the "y" above. this is an attested toponym in `lexicon lookup`

15.text: Euˊnmun I found a few dart-prongs made

16.text: of bone (Fig. 57). At Indian Point I came

17.text: across a small dart and a throwing-board;

18.text: but it was said that they came originally

19.text: from the American side (Fig. 58, c). The

20.text: Koryak of Penshina Bay in the Okhotsk

21.text: Sea, however, use throwing-boards and darts

22.text: of somewhat different shape for hunting both

23.text: birds and small seals. Those used on the

24.text: Anadyr (Fig. 58, a, b) and Kolyma have

25.text: a shaft about seven or eight feet long,

26.text: slender at the rear end, and thick at the

27.text: head. They have one central prong and

28.text: three circular prongs made of iron, and

29.text: fastened with sinew or twine. The Anadyr

30.text: throwing-board has a hole on the right side

31.text: for the forefinger; that of the Kolyma region

32.text: has the hole more frequently in the middle.

33.text: The Chukchee on the Chaun tundra often

34.text: use the bird-dart without the board, sending

35.text: it off simply from the hand.
